title: Microplastic in marine environment: reworking and optimisation of two analytical protocols for the extraction of microplastics from sediments and oysters
author: Rivoira, Castiglioni, et al.
materials: oxidation of lipids and organic matter;

steps.title: Prepare microplastic reference particles
steps.instruction: Obtain polymers representing common marine MPs: low‑density polyethylene (PE‑LD, ρ = 0.93 g cm⁻³), high‑density polyethylene caps (PE‑HD, ρ = 1.00 g cm⁻³), polyethylene terephthalate (PET, ρ = 1.38 g cm⁻³), polyamide (nylon 6, ρ = 1.13 g cm⁻³) and 1 mm high‑density polyethylene microspheres (ρ = 1.00 g cm⁻³, purchased from Cospheric). Produce all particles (except microspheres) in the laboratory from real items, then sieve through a 5 mm mesh to discard particles larger than 5 mm. Use microspheres as received.

steps.title: Create fortified sediment sample
steps.instruction: Weigh 10 mg of each MP type, count individual particles under a stereomicroscope, then add them to 100 g of sediment that has been sieved to ≤2 mm and dried at 90 °C overnight, to obtain a laboratory‑fortified sediment sample for method development.

steps.title: First density separation of sediment
steps.instruction: Perform the initial density‑separation step on the fortified (or environmental) sediment to separate MPs from the bulk matrix.

steps.title: Oxidize organic matter in sediment
steps.instruction: Treat the supernatant from the first density separation with an oxidizing agent (e.g., hydrogen peroxide) to digest organic matter that co‑floats with MPs.

steps.title: Second density separation of sediment
steps.instruction: Repeat the density‑separation step on the oxidized suspension to recover MPs.

steps.title: Iterative oxidation‑density cycles (if needed)
steps.instruction: If the sediment has a high organic‑matter content (e.g., bed sediments with ~5 % OM, versus sandy sediments with ~1 % OM), repeat the oxidation (step 4) and second density separation (step 5) until no visible organic residue remains.

steps.title: Inspect MPs under stereomicroscope
steps.instruction: Transfer the final MP concentrate to a petri dish and examine/quantify MPs using a stereomicroscope.

steps.title: Create fortified oyster sample
steps.instruction: Add 10 mg of each MP type to homogenized oyster tissue (which contains ~3 % lipids) to generate a laboratory‑fortified oyster sample for method testing.

steps.title: Oxidize lipids and organic matter in oysters
steps.instruction: Treat the oyster homogenate with an oxidizing agent (e.g., hydrogen peroxide) to digest lipids and other organic material.

steps.title: Density separation of oyster digest
steps.instruction: Perform a density‑separation step on the oxidized oyster solution to float MPs.

steps.title: Iterative oxidation‑density cycles for oysters
steps.instruction: If residual organic/fat material remains, repeat the oxidation (step 9) and density separation (step 10) until the supernatant is clear.

steps.title: Inspect oyster‑derived MPs
steps.instruction: Collect the MP fraction and examine/quantify under a stereomicroscope.

description: Several procedures are nowadays investigated for the extraction of microplastics (MPs) from marine environment, with peculiarities typical of each investigated matrix (water, sediment, biota, etc.). Two main steps in common for all the extraction procedures are generally the ones that need adaptation to the investigated matrix: i) a density separation, where MPs are separated from their matrix, exploiting differences in terms of density between an extraction solution and MP polymers; ii) oxidation of organic matter, that float with separated MPs, thus making difficult MPs extraction and recognition. Among the procedures already published, the NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) protocol is one of the most applied [1]. It includes procedures focused on the analysis of MPs in water and sediments developed for polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and polyester (PEs), not considering polyethylene terephthalate (PET), which is one of the most detected plastic in the environment [2]. On the contrary, no procedures for biota are there described. It was recently demonstrated how MPs, in particular fibres, can aggregate into clusters, thus becoming heavier and accumulating in marine sediments [3]. On the other hand, possible interactions of MPs with biota and in particular with bivalve organisms such as oysters, that are recognised to act like filters retaining marine pollutants, can occur [4], with possible MPs accumulation. Moving from such considerations, efficient methods for the extraction of MPs from sediments and oysters are highly attractive. Sediment composition greatly differs depending on the type of sediment.
